On August 3, 2026, President Trump accused ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE:XOM) and Chevron Corporation (NYSE:CVX) of making "too much money" off high fuel prices just three days after both companies reported blowout second-quarter earnings fueled by the ongoing Iran war. Trump told reporters, "Chevron, too much money. ExxonMobil, too much. Too much money," demanding the companies "give some of that back to the public." Chevron Corporation (NYSE:CVX)'s earnings soared nearly 400% to $12 billion, and ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE:XOM)'s more than doubled to $14.5 billion, both driven by crude prices that jumped after the U.S. and Israel struck Iran in February and Tehran retaliated by threatening the Strait of Hormuz. Gasoline prices have climbed nearly 40% since the war began, a real problem for Trump heading into November's midterm elections. Earlier Monday, Trump also publicly criticized Chevron CEO Mike Wirth on social media for not crediting his administration during a Fox News interview, writing that without "the genius, foresight, strength, and stability" of his administration, the oil industry "would be DEAD." This makes you wonder: Is Trump's political pressure a real threat to these huge oil profits, or just pre-election talk while prices are already sliding on hope the Iran conflict ends soon? For illustration purposes only. Photo by Kayden Moore on Pexels Chevron Corporation (NYSE:CVX)'s quarterly profit was its highest in at least six years, and the company's return to Venezuela stands out as a genuine growth story: it stayed in the country through nationalization in 2007 while Exxon and ConocoPhillips both exited, and Trump himself noted Chevron is "back, far bigger and stronger than ever before." However, Chevron shares fell about 2% after Trump's comments Monday, and the company now faces direct presidential pressure to cut prices even as it posts record results. Being singled out by name is a real reputational risk few oil executives want. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE:XOM)'s profit more than doubled year over year, showing just how much the Iran-driven price spike has boosted the industry's biggest player. The company still makes huge amounts of cash, even without a big comeback story like Chevron's. Still, Exxon shares also slipped after Trump's remarks. Unlike Chevron, Exxon left Venezuela in 2007, leaving it with fewer growth options besides high oil prices, which just dropped 5% on Monday as Iran tensions eased. Insider Monkey's hedge fund database shows Chevron had 103 hedge fund holders as of Q1 2026, up from 86 the quarter before, with the dollar value hedge funds held rising from about $26.3 billion to $29.6 billion. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE:XOM) had 94 holders, down from 98. Among refining peers, Valero had 67 holders, up from 65, and Marathon Petroleum had 54, down from 64. Chevron draws more hedge fund interest than Exxon and both refiners. Both companies just posted some of their best results in years, but the same war that delivered those profits has now put a target on their backs in Washington. Neither company controls how long that political pressure or the high oil prices behind it will last. Overall, Chevron Corporation (NYSE:CVX) wins since it draws more hedge fund interest than Exxon. On Agustus 11, 2026: price 194.91 USD, trend uptrend, RSI 59.5, support 181.60, resistance 196.83. technical analysis of cvx stock. CVX Testing Key Resistance… Chevron Corp. shares rose to 194.91 on the NYSE, up 4.48% from the previous close of 186.56, according to Yahoo Finance data cited at 10 August 2026 20:30 WIB. The move pushed the stock back into the upper end of its recent trading band, with price now sitting near the top of the 20-day range and just below the latest resistance zone. In plain terms, the market is paying up for CVX again, but the chart is now close to an area where sellers have recently shown up. The broader structure remains constructive. Chevron is still in an uptrend, helped by the SMA20 at 189.84 rising at a 1.74% pace over the past five days, while the SMA50 at 183.09 sits below it. That positioning matters because it shows the shorter-term average is already above the longer-term one, a classic sign that momentum has improved even without a fresh moving-average crossover. The absence of a new MA-cross means the rally is being extended rather than freshly triggered, which often makes the next test of resistance more important than the last breakout. The price is also trading above the middle Bollinger band at 189.84, with the upper band at 198.28 and the lower band at 181.40. That places CVX in the upper half of its volatility envelope, but not yet at an extreme. The stock is already at 87% of its 20-day range and has moved within striking distance of the 196.83 resistance level. That combination usually signals a market that is still trending, but one where follow-through needs to be proven rather than assumed. The oscillator picture is more mixed than the price trend. The RSI at 59.5 is neutral, which means the stock is neither stretched nor washed out. That is important: it leaves room for further gains, but it does not confirm a momentum surge. The Stochastic %K at 76.5 versus %D at 36.8 points to short-term strength, but the gap between the two lines also suggests the move may be getting ahead of itself. In practical terms, Stochastic above 70 often means price is nearer the top of its recent range, not that a reversal is guaranteed. The most cautionary signal comes from MACD at 2.647, which remains below its signal line at 2.973, leaving a -0.326 histogram. That negative histogram means upside momentum is still lagging the trend in price. So while the chart says Chevron is advancing, the oscillator setup says the advance has not yet fully re-accelerated. This is the kind of divergence traders watch when a stock climbs into resistance: price is strong, but the internal thrust is only moderate. Volatility is contained rather than explosive. The ATR at 4.98, equal to 2.6% of price, indicates a normal trading environment, not a disorderly one. The Bollinger band width of 8.9% is also described as normal, which suggests the stock is not in a squeeze that would foreshadow a sharp breakout, nor in an expansion phase that would imply unusually large swings. In other words, CVX has room to move, but the chart does not yet show the kind of compression that typically precedes a major directional release. Volume, however, is doing more of the talking. The latest session recorded 13,652,700 shares, about 1.7x the 20-session average of 7,856,580, and OBV is rising. That matters because rising volume alongside a price advance suggests participation is broad enough to support the move. If the rally had come on thin trading, it would have looked more fragile. Instead, the surge in turnover says institutions and larger market participants likely had a hand in the day’s strength. The nearest support sits at 181.60, just above the lower Bollinger band at 181.40. That confluence is meaningful: if price loses that area, the chart would be signaling that the recent rebound has failed to hold its own volatility floor. On the upside, 196.83 is the immediate resistance to watch, while the broader three-month high stands at 198.87. Those two levels form a tight overhead zone, and the market is now close enough that the next move could decide whether CVX pauses, breaks through, or rolls back into the middle of its range. If Chevron clears 196.83 decisively, the chart would be pointing toward a retest of the 198.87 three-month high. If it fails there, a retreat toward 189.84 would fit a normal pullback to the Bollinger midline and the SMA20. If that fails, the 181.60 support becomes the key line separating a healthy consolidation from a deeper unwind. HOLD (wait & see) is the clearest reading from the current setup. - Reason 1: Price is in an uptrend and above both the SMA20 and SMA50, which supports the trend.
- Reason 2: Volume and OBV are confirming participation, so the move is not isolated.
- Reason 3: MACD remains below its signal line, showing momentum is still not fully aligned with the price advance. - Verdict invalidated if price breaks below 181.60, because that would damage the current support structure and put the lower Bollinger band in play. - Ideal Entry Range: 189.84 to 181.60 on a pullback that holds the SMA20 and support zone.
- Exit Target: 196.83, with 198.87 as the next chart reference if resistance gives way.
- Stop Loss protection: below 181.40 to 181.60, using the lower Bollinger band and nearby support as the risk boundary. For non-traders: the chart is still healthy, but CVX is close enough to resistance that it makes more sense to wait for confirmation than to assume the next move will be upward. Chevron Corporation (NYSE:CVX - Get Free Report)'s share price shot up 4.3% during mid-day trading on Monday . The company traded as high as $194.99 and last traded at $194.57. Approximately 11,921,317 shares were traded  during trading, an increase of 8% from the average daily volume of 11,037,087 shares. The stock had previously closed at $186.56. Here are the key news stories impacting Chevron this week: A number of research firms have recently weighed in on CVX. The Goldman Sachs Group  restated a "buy" rating and issued a $216.00 target price on shares of Chevron in a report on Wednesday, May 6th. TD Cowen lifted their price target on Chevron from $200.00 to $205.00 and gave the stock a "hold" rating in a research report on Wednesday, August 5th. Piper Sandler began coverage on Chevron in a research report on Thursday, July 23rd. They issued an "overweight" rating and a $207.00 price target for the company. Scotiabank boosted their price objective on Chevron from $168.00 to $187.00 and gave the stock a "sector perform" rating in a research note on Wednesday, April 22nd. Finally, Mizuho  set a $224.00 price objective on Chevron in a research report on Monday, August 3rd. Eighteen equities research analysts have rated the stock with a Buy rating, six have assigned  a Hold rating and one  has given a Sell rating to the company's stock. According to data from MarketBeat, Chevron presently has a consensus rating of "Moderate Buy" and a consensus price target of $207.48. The firm has a market cap of $384.43 billion, a P/E ratio of 18.65, a PEG ratio of 0.57 and a beta of 0.49. The company has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.19, a current ratio of 1.25 and a quick ratio of 0.98. The stock's 50-day simple moving average is $182.37 and its two-hundred day simple moving average is $185.94. Chevron (NYSE:CVX - Get Free Report) last released its earnings results on Friday, July 31st. The oil and gas company reported $6.06 earnings per share (EPS) for the quarter, topping the consensus estimate of $5.55 by $0.51. Chevron had a net margin of 9.57% and a return on equity of 11.09%. The firm had revenue of $67.20 billion during the quarter, compared to analyst estimates of $62.72 billion. During the same quarter last year, the business earned $1.77 EPS. The business's revenue was up 57.4% on a year-over-year basis.  Equities research analysts forecast that  Chevron Corporation will post 15.86 earnings per share for the current fiscal year. The company also recently disclosed a quarterly dividend, which will be paid on Thursday, September 10th. Shareholders of record on Wednesday, August 19th will be paid a $1.78 dividend. The ex-dividend date of this dividend is Wednesday, August 19th. This represents a $7.12 annualized dividend and a yield of 3.7%. Chevron's dividend payout ratio (DPR) is presently 68.26%. In other news, CEO Michael K. Wirth sold 5,547 shares of the stock in a transaction that occurred on Wednesday, August 5th. The stock was sold at an average price of $187.00, for a total value of $1,037,289.00. Following the sale, the chief executive officer directly owned 26,308 shares in the company, valued at approximately $4,919,596. This represents a 17.41% decrease in their ownership of the stock. The sale was disclosed in a filing with the SEC, which can be accessed through the SEC website. Also, Director John B. Hess sold 100,000 shares of the firm's stock in a transaction that occurred on Monday, August 3rd. The stock was sold at an average price of $194.26, for a total value of $19,426,000.00. Following the sale, the director directly owned 178,045 shares of the company's stock, valued at $34,587,021.70. This represents a 35.97% decrease in their ownership of the stock. The disclosure for this sale is available in the SEC filing. In the last three months, insiders sold 1,196,212 shares of company stock valued at $231,819,366. 0.56% of the stock is owned by insiders. Several hedge funds have recently bought and sold shares of the business. Midwest Capital Advisors LLC purchased a new position in  Chevron in the 1st quarter worth about $25,000.  Main Street Group LTD purchased a new stake in  Chevron in the 1st quarter valued at about $28,000.  Phillip James Consulting Co. bought a new position in  Chevron in the 4th quarter worth about $26,000.  Core Wealth Advisors LLC purchased a new position in shares of  Chevron during the fourth quarter worth approximately $26,000.  Finally, Karpus Management Inc. purchased a new position in shares of  Chevron during the fourth quarter worth approximately $27,000. Institutional investors own  72.42% of the company's stock. Chevron Corporation NYSE: CVX is an American multinational energy company engaged in virtually all aspects of the oil and gas industry. As an integrated energy firm, Chevron's core activities include upstream oil and natural gas exploration and production, midstream transportation and storage, downstream refining and marketing of fuels and lubricants, and petrochemical manufacturing through joint ventures and subsidiaries. The company markets fuels under brands such as Chevron, Texaco and Caltex and supplies a range of products and services to retail customers, industrial users and commercial fleets worldwide. Chevron traces its corporate lineage to the early petroleum companies that eventually became Standard Oil of California and has evolved through significant mergers and restructurings, including the acquisitions of Gulf Oil and Texaco. title: Can Chevron's Hess Synergies Extend Growth and Lift Cash Flow Further? - Yahoo Finance Singapore
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Chevron Corporation CVX reaches the one-year anniversary of its Hess acquisition with integration benefits running ahead of plan. Chevron has exceeded its original synergy target, strengthening the case that Hess can contribute more than additional production. The next test is durability. Investors will be watching whether the acquired assets can keep supporting free cash flow, per-share accretion and Chevron's production-growth objectives through 2030. Chevron achieved $1.5 billion of annual run-rate Hess synergies within one year of closing, six months ahead of schedule. The amount was 50% above its initial target, showing that integration benefits have arrived faster and at a larger scale than first expected. That speed matters because the transaction's value depends on operational execution after closing. ConocoPhillips COP offers a relevant industry comparison, having completed the integration of Marathon Oil and reported more than $1 billion of run-rate synergy capture in 2025. Large upstream deals are increasingly judged on how quickly scale converts into lower costs and better returns. The Hess assets are contributing more than barrels. Management said they are generating strong free cash flow that is roughly double the incremental dividends associated with the acquisition. Chevron also said the acquired assets are accretive on a per-share basis. That supports the view that the combination is enhancing financial output rather than merely expanding the company's asset count. Worldwide net oil-equivalent production reached 4.07 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, up 20% year over year. The increase primarily reflected legacy Hess assets alongside growth in the Permian Basin and Gulf of America. A larger production base gives Chevron more volume from which to generate future cash flow when commodity conditions are supportive. U.S. production also reached a record 2.08 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, reinforcing the scale of the enlarged upstream portfolio. Guyana gives Chevron a longer-dated growth engine. Management expects the asset to extend high-margin oil growth into the 2030s, while the company remains confident in its broader target of 2%-3% annual production growth through 2030. Exxon Mobil Corporation XOM, the operator of Guyana's Stabroek Block, holds a 45% interest and has continued advancing offshore developments there. For Chevron, the investment case rests on translating its Hess-derived Guyana exposure and other growth assets into sustained portfolio expansion. Hess integration can improve Chevron's cost structure and asset mix, but it cannot remove commodity-price exposure. Second-quarter 2026 results benefited from an average Brent price of $104 per barrel, compared with $68 a year earlier. If oil or gas realizations weaken materially, production growth may not fully offset the pressure on earnings and cash flow. Chevron also remains exposed to project execution, geopolitical disruption and the challenge of sustaining expected benefits from the acquisition. Chevron has pulled forward meaningful Hess benefits, expanded production and added longer-duration growth through Guyana. Those factors strengthen the company's operating and cash-flow foundation, but future gains still depend on execution and commodity conditions. The A scores indicate favorable characteristics across the major investment styles, while the Hold rank supports a measured stance. Chevron's commodity sensitivity and premium valuation relative to most peers remain reasons to weigh further Hess-driven gains carefully. The update, which showed stronger revenue and a healthier operating margin than the prior comparable period, has reinforced the company's standing among market participants who track steady, cash-generative names in the energy patch. That framing matters this week in particular, because major indices are hovering close to all-time marks even as pockets of the technology trade show visible strain, creating a market backdrop in which energy value names are being examined with fresh interest. Energy majors have spent recent stretches navigating a market defined by swinging crude prices, uneven refining margins, and a structural pivot toward electrification that has forced long-established producers to rethink how they allocate capital. Against that backdrop, a name with the scale and diversification of the company in focus tends to draw scrutiny not because it is flashy, but because it is steady. The energy sector as a whole has been treated by many market participants as a place to find durable cash generation rather than rapid expansion, and that framing has only strengthened as broader equity benchmarks have climbed to levels that leave many growth-oriented names looking stretched on a pricing basis. The quarterly update that landed recently gave this narrative another data point. Rather than showing strain from a choppy commodity backdrop, the company posted figures that pointed toward resilience, a description that market watchers have increasingly applied to integrated energy operators capable of absorbing swings in crude pricing through the balance of upstream production, midstream logistics, and downstream refining. That resilience is precisely the quality that tends to appeal to those weighing energy names through a value lens rather than a momentum one. Understanding why this update carried the weight it did requires stepping back to look at how the business actually operates. The company runs an integrated model spanning upstream exploration and production, a global network of refining and chemical assets, and a marketing arm that touches fuel retail in numerous regions. This structure is deliberate. When crude pricing softens, the downstream refining and chemicals side can act as a partial offset, since lower input costs can support margin even as upstream revenue per barrel declines. When crude pricing firms, the upstream side captures the benefit directly. That built-in balance is part of why integrated majors are often treated differently from pure-play exploration names when market participants assess resilience through cycles. Operationally, the company has also leaned into large-scale, long-life projects that are designed to generate steady output over extended periods rather than short bursts tied to a single commodity cycle. This includes deepwater developments, liquefied natural gas infrastructure, and a growing footprint in some of the lowest-cost production basins globally. The logic behind this positioning is straightforward: assets with lower breakeven costs tend to remain economically viable across a wider range of crude pricing environments, which in turn supports steadier cash generation and, by extension, steadier capital distribution to equity owners. The recent quarterly disclosure did more than simply beat the prior comparable period on a top-line basis. It also showed an operating margin that improved relative to the same stretch a year earlier, an outcome that tends to carry particular weight in the energy sector because margin performance there is often treated as a proxy for how well a company is managing costs, throughput, and mix even when commodity pricing itself is not moving dramatically in one direction. Sentiment around the name firmed measurably in the aftermath, with market commentary framing the update as evidence that capital discipline exercised over recent periods was translating into tangible earnings strength. That kind of reporting season narrative tends to matter more for value-oriented energy names than for growth names, precisely because the market participants who gravitate toward this corner of the sector are typically weighing steady execution against a backdrop of modest pricing multiples. A quarter that reinforces the case for durable cash generation, rather than one that surprises with a dramatic swing in either direction, tends to be read as confirmation of an existing narrative rather than a reason to substantially reprice the stock. That appears to be roughly how the market treated this particular update, with firmer sentiment following the release rather than a dramatic repricing event. One of the more closely watched elements of any energy major's quarterly disclosure is what happens with cash returned to equity owners. In this case, the company maintained its cash distribution, extending a long streak of consistent payouts that has become a defining feature of its reputation among market participants who track energy value names specifically for their capital discipline. Maintaining a distribution through a period of commodity volatility signals confidence in underlying cash generation, and it also reflects a broader capital allocation stance that has prioritized steady payouts and disciplined spending over aggressive expansion. This approach stands in contrast to earlier eras of the energy sector, when producers were more inclined to chase output growth aggressively during periods of firm commodity pricing, only to face strain when conditions reversed. The current generation of energy majors, including the company profiled here, has generally shifted toward a framework that prioritizes free cash generation, measured capital spending, and steady distribution to equity owners over rapid volume growth. That shift has been part of what has made energy value names more palatable to market participants who prioritize durability over rapid appreciation, and the maintained distribution in the latest update reinforces that this approach remains intact. Beyond company-specific results, the broader environment for crude and refined products continues to shape how energy value names are read by the market. Global crude conditions have remained comparatively steady in recent stretches, without the kind of dramatic supply disruption or demand collapse that has periodically rattled the sector in past cycles. Refining conditions, meanwhile, have held at levels that continue to support healthy throughput economics across much of the industry, providing a supportive backdrop for integrated operators with meaningful downstream exposure. This steadiness matters because energy value names tend to be judged less on whether commodity pricing is rising sharply and more on whether the operating environment is stable enough to support consistent execution. A market defined by wild commodity swings tends to make it harder for market participants to have confidence in near-term earnings trajectories, whereas a steadier backdrop allows companies with strong operational execution to demonstrate that execution more clearly. The current environment, characterized by measured global crude conditions and healthy refining economics, appears to be providing exactly that kind of setting for names like the one at the center of this update. One of the more notable structural themes shaping how the market views energy names this year has little to do with crude pricing directly and everything to do with electricity. The rapid build-out of artificial-intelligence infrastructure, particularly large data-center campuses designed to support intensive computing workloads, has driven a level of power demand that many grid operators and energy suppliers did not anticipate even a few years back. This has created a new and somewhat unexpected driver of interest in traditional energy names, since natural gas in particular has emerged as a favored fuel source for meeting incremental power needs tied to this build-out. For an integrated energy major with meaningful natural gas production and infrastructure, this dynamic represents a structural driver worth watching closely, even though it sits somewhat apart from the traditional narrative around crude pricing and refining margins. Market participants have increasingly begun weighing how exposed different energy names are to this power-demand theme, and companies with flexible natural gas supply positions are being examined with particular interest as a result. This is one of several threads knitting together what might otherwise look like separate stories, namely the steady performance of legacy energy majors and the rapid expansion of computing infrastructure tied to artificial intelligence. Refining and chemicals operations remain a critical piece of the puzzle for understanding how an integrated energy major generates earnings across a full cycle. Downstream margin dynamics are shaped by a combination of factors, including the spread between crude input costs and finished product pricing, the utilization rates achieved across a refining network, and the mix of products a given set of facilities is configured to produce. In recent periods, refining margins across much of the industry have held at levels that continue to support healthy downstream earnings, providing a meaningful complement to upstream production revenue. That contrast, chip-sector wobbles set against software-sector strength, has left parts of the market feeling unsettled even as headline indices sit near their highs. The company's recent quarterly update, landing at a moment when broader market sentiment is somewhat mixed beneath the surface, has reinforced its positioning as one of the names market participants point to when discussing where durable value can still be found within a market that is otherwise testing new highs. Looking beyond the immediate quarterly update, several structural themes continue to shape how energy majors, and the company in particular, are likely to be examined by the market in coming periods. The pace of the global energy transition remains a persistent thread, with companies across the sector continuing to balance traditional hydrocarbon production against measured capital deployment toward lower-carbon initiatives. How aggressively, or conservatively, a given company pursues that balance continues to factor into how market participants assess long-term positioning. Power demand tied to artificial-intelligence infrastructure represents another structural theme likely to remain relevant well beyond the current reporting season, given the scale of data-center build-out programs currently underway across the country. Natural gas supply flexibility, in particular, is likely to remain a differentiator among energy majors as this theme continues to unfold. Meanwhile, global crude supply dynamics, including production decisions made by major exporting nations, will continue to shape the pricing backdrop against which integrated majors are measured. Taken together, these threads indicate that the current period of relative steadiness in the sector, and the firmer sentiment that has followed the latest update, will likely continue to be tested by a combination of commodity pricing shifts, energy transition dynamics, and the ongoing build-out of power-intensive computing infrastructure. title: Chevron Stock Jumps 3.3% as Hormuz Doubts Lift Oil - TradingView
content: Chevron CVX, the integrated energy heavyweight pumping oil and running refineries around the world, delivered $12.1 billion of second-quarter earnings before its shares jumped roughly 3.3% Monday morning. But this move is about more than one strong quarter. Brent crude was back near $85 per barrel as hopes for a quick reopening of the Strait of Hormuz took another hit, with Iran putting conditions on restoring shipping traffic. That flipped the oil trade fast. Crude had tumbled more than 7% the previous week as investors bet on diplomacy. Now geopolitical risk is back on the screen, and Chevron suddenly has a much stronger oil-price tailwind behind already booming production. The numbers show just how much firepower Chevron has if crude stays elevated. Production reached roughly 4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, including a record 2.08 million barrels from the U.S. Upstream earnings hit $8.2 billion, while downstream profit climbed to $4.9 billion as stronger refining margins kicked in. U.S. refineries processed more than 1 million barrels per day, another record. That is the setup investors want from an integrated oil giant: more barrels, stronger refining economics and higher crude prices hitting at the same time. Add the Hess integration and $6.5 billion returned through dividends and buybacks during the quarter, and Chevron has a serious cash machine working underneath the geopolitical headlines. There is one catch: the stock is no bargain. GuruFocus puts Chevron at $192.63 versus a GF Value estimate of $158.06, meaning the shares trade about 21.87% above GF Value. That is a chunky premium, and it raises the bar from here. If oil stays high, record production keeps climbing and Hess delivers the expected boost, Chevron could grow into that valuation. If Hormuz tensions fade and crude rolls over, investors are suddenly holding an expensive oil stock into a weaker commodity tape. Chevron has the production, the cash flow and the oil-price momentum. Chevron Corporation CVX has entered the second half of 2026 with considerable operating momentum. The company recently delivered an impressive quarterly beat, reporting adjusted earnings of $12 billion for the second quarter of 2026. The strong performance was supported by solid operational execution, higher crude oil price realizations, robust refining margins and increased production following the Hess acquisition. Results were further underpinned by stronger cash flow, a resilient upstream portfolio and disciplined shareholder returns. Yet with shares lagging both ExxonMobil XOM and Shell SHEL, and valuation sitting at a premium, the bigger question is whether this momentum can translate into meaningful upside for investors. Chevron's second-quarter operating performance was impressive. Worldwide net oil-equivalent production reached 4.07 million barrels per day, up 20% year over year, driven largely by legacy Hess assets and growth in the Permian Basin and Gulf of America. U.S. production reached a record 2.07 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. Refining operations were similarly strong, with U.S. crude unit throughput reaching a record 1.07 million barrels per day and utilization exceeding 97%. Higher commodity prices amplified those operating gains. Chevron reported second-quarter earnings of $12.1 billion, or $6.11 per share, while adjusted earnings totaled roughly $12 billion, or $6.06 per share. Cash flow from operations excluding working capital was $19.7 billion, while adjusted free cash flow reached $15.4 billion. That cash generation has provided significant financial flexibility. Chevron reduced debt by a record $8.4 billion during the quarter, while its net debt-to-CFFO ratio improved to 0.6X. At the same time, the company continued returning capital, paying $3.5 billion of dividends and repurchasing $3 billion of shares during the quarter. The Hess acquisition is also showing tangible benefits. One year after closing, Chevron had captured $1.5 billion of annual run-rate synergies — 50% above its initial target and six months ahead of schedule. Management said the acquired assets are generating free cash flow at roughly twice the incremental dividend burden, while Guyana provides exposure to high-margin production growth extending into the 2030s. Cost discipline offers another lever. Chevron achieved $3 billion of annual run-rate structural cost reductions six months early, with more than 70% of the savings stemming from efficiency improvements. Meanwhile, management expects 2026 shale and tight capital spending per barrel of oil equivalent to be 25% below last year, indicating that production growth is becoming more capital efficient. Chevron is also broadening its opportunity set beyond conventional oil and gas. Project Kilby in West Texas includes a 20-year take-or-pay agreement to supply Microsoft with 2.67 gigawatts of behind-the-meter power. Management expects the project to generate mid-teens returns and long-duration cash flows that are less correlated with commodity cycles, although the project remains subject to final investment decision and execution. Commodity exposure remains the biggest swing factor. Chevron estimates that every $1 change in Brent affects full-year after-tax earnings and cash flow by roughly $600 million. Second-quarter Brent averaged nearly $104 per barrel, providing a substantial earnings tailwind that may not persist. Near-term operations also face maintenance headwinds. Chevron expects third-quarter upstream turnarounds and downtime to reduce production by 150,000-200,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, while downstream maintenance could reduce after-tax earnings by $175-$225 million. Geopolitical exposure, particularly around Kazakhstan's CPC export route and the Middle East, adds another layer of uncertainty. The company itself identifies commodity prices, OPEC+ actions, geopolitical conflicts and operational disruptions among material risks. Chevron's shares have gained 1% over the past three months compared with the sub-industry's 0.3% growth. However, the company underperformed its peers, as ExxonMobil and Shell have risen 2.2% and 3.7%, respectively, during the same time period. Chevron's premium valuation also leaves less room for error. The stock trades at roughly a 12.61X forward price-to-earnings multiple, notably higher than Shell's 9.44X but below ExxonMobil's 13.32X. Chevron's underlying picture is constructive: record production, accelerating Hess synergies, structural cost reductions, robust cash generation and a stronger balance sheet provide a solid foundation. The Microsoft power agreement also introduces an intriguing source of contracted, commodity-diversified growth. However, elevated commodity sensitivity and upcoming maintenance could create earnings volatility after an exceptionally strong second quarter. For now, Chevron, currently carrying a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), appears well positioned operationally, but investors may want clearer evidence that recent earnings strength can endure through a less supportive commodity environment before taking a more bullish stance. Even after that advance, valuation measures based on cash generation and business performance suggest the market may not fully reflect Chevrons longer-term financial capacity. As a major constituent of the S&P 500, Chevron now faces a key test: whether durable cash flows, disciplined operations, and emerging data center energy demand can support its valuation narrative. Chevrons valuation story is closely connected to the substantial cash generated by its global energy operations. Cash flow-based valuation models attempt to estimate what a business could be worth by examining the money it may generate for shareholders over time. Recent valuation analysis suggests Chevrons implied intrinsic value remains above its market valuation under this approach. That creates an interesting contrast because the companys shares have already delivered substantial gains over a multiyear period. The central issue is therefore less about past market performance and more about the durability of future cash generation. Energy prices, production volumes, operating discipline, project execution, and capital requirements can all influence that outcome. Chevrons scale provides exposure to multiple parts of the global energy system. Its upstream operations produce oil and natural gas, while downstream activities include refining and related energy businesses. This diversified structure can help the company navigate changing conditions across commodity markets. Artificial intelligence is creating an unusual new dimension for traditional energy companies. Rapid expansion of data centers is increasing electricity requirements, placing greater attention on reliable power and fuel supplies. Chevron has been positioning its operations to participate in this evolving demand environment. Long-term energy arrangements connected with AI-focused infrastructure could broaden the companys future commercial opportunities beyond conventional transportation and industrial energy demand. The development also shows why Chevron remains a closely watched  energy stock. AI may be associated primarily with semiconductor and software companies, but the physical infrastructure supporting advanced computing requires enormous amounts of dependable energy. For Chevron, that creates an opportunity to connect its traditional energy expertise with one of the fastest-developing areas of the digital economy. Cash flow analysis is only one way to assess Chevron. Valuation based on earnings presents a somewhat different picture. Chevron trades at a valuation premium compared with parts of the broader oil and gas industry. Ordinarily, that could suggest the market already recognizes some of the companys quality, scale, financial strength, and operating advantages. However, estimates of a valuation multiple considered appropriate for Chevrons business profile remain above its current market multiple in the supplied analysis. That leaves room for a constructive valuation interpretation even though Chevron does not appear inexpensive against every conventional industry comparison. The difference highlights an important point about valuation. A company can look relatively expensive compared with industry peers while appearing reasonably valued when assessed against its own expected cash generation, profitability, scale, and risk profile. Chevrons connection to expanding data center infrastructure could become increasingly important if artificial intelligence continues driving electricity consumption. The companys Project Kilby agreement with Microsoft is particularly relevant to this theme. Microsoft is a global technology company operating cloud computing, software, artificial intelligence, and digital infrastructure businesses. The arrangement illustrates how energy producers and technology companies can increasingly intersect as computing infrastructure expands. For Chevron, such agreements could provide another source of long-duration energy demand. They may also strengthen visibility around future cash flows if commercial arrangements translate into dependable recurring demand. Still, data center opportunities represent only part of Chevrons broader business. Commodity conditions, geopolitical developments, project costs, refining conditions, and global economic activity remain important factors affecting performance. Chevrons valuation case is therefore more nuanced than a simple declaration that the shares appear inexpensive or expensive. Cash flow-based analysis presents a constructive picture because estimated intrinsic value remains above the prevailing market valuation in the supplied assessment. Earnings-based analysis also indicates that Chevrons current multiple remains below a modeled fair multiple, although the company trades above some broader industry comparisons. At the same time, strong historical share performance raises the standard for future execution. Continued market strength would increasingly depend on Chevron maintaining cash generation, managing major projects effectively, and adapting its energy portfolio as demand patterns evolve. Political scrutiny surrounding energy industry profitability could also influence market sentiment. Regulatory changes, energy policy, taxation, and environmental requirements remain factors capable of reshaping expectations for major integrated energy companies. Chevron enters its next phase with considerable operating scale, strong cash-generating capabilities, and exposure to emerging energy requirements created by artificial intelligence infrastructure. The key valuation question is whether those advantages can translate into durable financial performance. Cash flow models provide an encouraging interpretation, while comparative multiples introduce additional nuance. Rather than offering a straightforward valuation conclusion, Chevrons current position highlights the tension between strong historical performance and expectations for future execution. Data center energy demand adds another dimension to that equation, but the durability of Chevrons underlying energy operations remains central to its longer-term market story. title: There's a 58% Chance of a Fed Rate Hike in October. These Are Stocks to Buy Anyway. - The Globe and Mail
content: UnitedHealth's comeback shouldn't be derailed by a potential rate hike. JPMorgan Chase's net investment income would increase with higher rates. Chevron's business would almost certainly be booming in an environment where rate hikes were needed. Many investors breathed a sigh of relief when the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) chose to leave rates unchanged at its latest meeting. However, the reprieve might not last long. CME Group's (NASDAQ: CME) FedWatch estimates the probability that the FOMC will increase rates in its next meeting in mid-September at 44.1%, based on 30-day Fed funds futures prices. FedWatch projects a 57.7% chance of a rate hike at the FOMC meeting scheduled for late October. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Rising rates are usually bad for many stocks. That isn't the case for all of them, though. Here are stocks to buy even if a rate increase is right around the corner. I'd put UnitedHealth Group(NYSE: UNH) high on the list of stocks to buy even if rate hikes are in store. Americans can't afford to cancel their health insurance just because the Fed increases the federal funds rate by 25 or 50 basis points. Importantly, UnitedHealth's turnaround appears to be the real deal. The health insurance stock is up more than 20% year to date. UnitedHealth's earnings jumped roughly 54% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. Management raised the company's full-year guidance due to the improving outlook. Bank stocks actually benefit from higher rates because they boost net interest income -- the spread between what banks charge borrowers and what they pay depositors. JPMorgan Chase(NYSE: JPM) ranks as the world's largest bank by market cap, so it stands to benefit more than most. JPMorgan's net interest income totaled $25.6 billion in Q2, up 10% year over year. Should the FOMC raise rates in October, look for this financial services giant to make even more money. Why might the Fed be forced to raise rates? Resurging inflation. And why is inflation higher than it was earlier this year? Higher fuel prices due primarily to the Iran war. Oil stocks have been solid winners in 2026 because of these dynamics. Chevron(NYSE: CVX) is no exception, with its shares up more than 20% year to date. If the FOMC votes to raise rates in October (or at any of its meetings during the rest of the year), it will likely be due to sustained high fuel prices keeping overall inflation elevated. Chevron's business should be humming along nicely in such an environment, making its stock attractive to investors seeking safe havens amid rising rates. A 58% probability of a rate hike implies a 42% chance that rates won't rise. How would UnitedHealth Group, JPMorgan Chase, and Chevron perform if rates remain flat or even decrease? Probably pretty well. UnitedHealth is relatively rate-neutral, but its momentum should continue no matter what the Fed does. JPMorgan's investment banking and asset management units would likely benefit if rates don't rise. Chevron's shares could decline somewhat if oil prices fall (which would be likely in a no-rate-hike scenario). However, the stock is still a solid long-term pick. Chevron stock has delivered a very strong 5 year run, yet current checks suggest the market price may still sit below what recent cash flow and earnings based valuations imply. The issue now is whether Chevron's recent share price still offers enough margin between market price and intrinsic value to justify fresh capital from investors who already see how strong the last 5 years have been. Find out why Chevron's 25.4% return over the last year is lagging behind its peers. The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model estimates what Chevron should be worth based on the cash it can return to shareholders over time. For Chevron, the latest twelve month free cash flow is about $27.2b, and the model assumes these cash flows continue to grow rather than shrink. On that basis, the 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to Equity model points to an estimated intrinsic value of about $369 per share. This compares to a current share price that implies a discount of roughly 49.5%. In other words, Chevron screens as undervalued on this DCF view. Chevron's long term gas supply deals with AI focused data centers, such as the Project Kilby agreement with Microsoft, help explain why some investors see support for those future cash flows even as the market price lags the model output. Overall, the DCF work suggests Chevron stock currently looks undervalued relative to the cash flow it is expected to generate. The P/E ratio is a useful way to see what investors are paying for each dollar of Chevron earnings. Chevron currently trades on about 17.8x earnings, which is above the Oil and Gas industry average of roughly 12.9x and also above the peer group average of about 15.2x. Simply Wall St's fair P/E for Chevron is higher, at around 25.5x, based on its mix of size, profitability and risk. That is a sizeable gap to the current 17.8x multiple, even though the stock already trades at a premium to the broader industry. On this framework, the market is pricing Chevron below what its earnings profile would typically support. On the P/E multiple, Chevron stock appears undervalued relative to what the fair ratio suggests investors might usually pay for its earnings.
